body:
TASK-168 needs an advisor status reset — its shelve was my infrastructure, not the spec

Asking rather than doing, because promoting NeedsAttention to Approved is your gate and I am not going to route around it.

TASK-168 is parked NeedsAttention on a shelve that has nothing to do with the work. What happened, verified from the drain log, the events feed, the lease file and the codex headless log rather than inferred:

The 10:53 drain launched the implementer for TASK-168 at 13:36:14 local, lease 01a0bb6261fe, scope TASK-1-144, worktree aida-task168. The codex session got as far as reading review_verdict.rs and was killed mid-exploration when I swapped the drain launcher and tore down the parent process group. nohup guards SIGHUP, not a group kill, so the drain and its codex child died together. Its headless log stops mid-item with fourteen lines and no result.

The relaunched drain then burned both retries in fifteen seconds — attempt 1 six seconds, attempt 2 nine — because lease 01a0bb6261fe was still held on scope TASK-1-144. It reported that as "could not match the orchestrated session (claude id 01a0bb64) to a session lease", which is a true statement about the wrong thing and sent me looking at session-id matching for twenty minutes before the lease listing showed the real cause.

I have released the orphaned lease, removed the stale aida-task168 worktree and deleted task-168-work. The branch carried no commits against origin/main, so nothing was stranded and nothing was lost. The spec is unstarted and clean. A comment recording all of this is already on it.

THE ASK: aida edit TASK-168 --status approved. It is already routed on role:implementer, so it will be picked up on the next wave once the status allows it.

TWO THINGS WORTH A SPEC, your call on whether they are one or two:

A drain restart cannot reclaim a lease its own previous run orphaned. The batch drive carries no --steal, so any drain death mid-implementer poisons that spec for the whole retry budget. Either the drain should steal a lease whose recorded pid is dead, or a dead-pid lease should not block a fresh claim at all. This is generic — an OOM kill or a machine reboot produces the identical shape, and then it is nobody's launcher swap.

The error message misdirects. "Could not match the orchestrated session to a session lease" describes the symptom; the cause is "the previous attempt's lease is still held on this scope". The code already lists candidate lease ids as diagnostics; it could instead notice that one of them holds THIS spec's scope and say so.

I am not filing these myself since they are orchestrator behaviour and you own that call.
